top10.insight: Overtime is the single strongest attrition driver in the dataset: 30.53% of overtime workers leave versus 10.44% of non-overtime workers (2.9x), and the 416 overtime employees (28.3% of headcount) supply 127 of 237 leavers — 53.6% of ALL attrition. Its chi-square (87.6) edges out even JobRole (86.2).

top10.recommendation: Make OverTime the top-level filter on the attrition dashboard and launch an overtime-governance program (mandatory OT approval, workload rebalancing, comp-off); if the 416 OT workers left at the non-OT rate of 10.44%, expected leavers drop from 127 to ~43 — roughly 84 fewer exits, a 35% cut in total company attrition.

top10.insight: Risk is multiplicative, not additive: OverTime + JobLevel 1 churns at 52.56% (82 of 156) — roughly double either factor alone (JL1 26.34%, OT 30.53%) — and this 10.6%-of-headcount segment produces 34.6% of all company attrition; the closely overlapping OverTime + tenure <=2 years cell runs 50.96% (53 of 104), meaning every second overtime-loaded new joiner is lost.

top10.insight: The lowest income band is the concentration point and overtime turns it into near-certain churn: the <$2.5K band holds 226 employees (15.4% of 1470) yet supplies 77 of 237 leavers (32.5%) at 34.07%, and the OverTime + Income<$2.5K cell loses 48 of 70 people (68.57%) — the worst segment in the entire dataset, where an employee is more likely to leave than to stay.

top10.insight: Single-KPI, rate-ranked reporting systematically misallocates leadership attention: the 16.12% headline conceals an 8.3x internal spread (68.57% in the worst cell vs 8.24% for No-OT JobLevel>=3); rate-ranking points executives at Sales (20.63%) while R&D supplies 133 of 237 leavers (56.1% of all replacement cost) at a below-average 13.84%; and of four pay fields only MonthlyIncome discriminates (corr -0.16, p=4.43e-13) — HourlyRate (p=0.791) and MonthlyRate (p=0.565) are pure noise, as is gender (p=0.291).

final.narrative:
The headline number — 237 leavers out of 1,470 employees, a 16.12% attrition rate — looks like a moderate, company-wide problem. It is neither. Beneath the average sits an 8.3x spread in risk: the safest population (no overtime, JobLevel 3+) loses just 8.24% of its people, while the worst cell — overtime workers earning under $2,500 a month — loses 68.57%, meaning those employees are literally more likely to leave than to stay. The losses are ferociously concentrated: 53.6% of all leavers come from the 28.3% of staff working overtime; 60% come from just three low-paid frontline roles (Laboratory Technician, Research Scientist, Sales Representative — 142 of 237 leavers); 65% hold zero stock options; 31.6% are in their first year; and 67.5% are aged 35 or under. This is not a workforce problem — it is a small number of identifiable, junior, underpaid, overworked pockets bleeding out at coin-flip rates while recruiting and onboarding investment is written off before it pays back.

The drivers are clear and they compound multiplicatively. Overtime is the single strongest factor in the dataset (30.53% vs 10.44%, chi-square 87.6), and when layered on low pay or junior level it roughly doubles: OT + income under $2.5K hits 68.57%, OT + JobLevel 1 hits 52.56% (82 leavers — over a third of company attrition from 156 people), and OT in the first two years hits 50.96%. Pay itself follows a clean gradient — 34.07% attrition below $2.5K falling to 3.76% at $15-20K — and within the frontline roles the leavers were specifically the underpaid ones (12-28% below stayer medians), while senior leavers actually out-earned stayers, proving two different problems need two different budgets. The 0-to-1 stock option step alone coincides with a drop from 24.41% to 9.4%. Just as important is what is NOT driving attrition: promotion stagnation (p=0.199 — long-stagnant veterans are the most loyal cohort at 13.79%), gender (p=0.291), and salary hikes, which are statistically identical for leavers and stayers (p=0.614) — which is why the company loses 37 top-rated performers a year at the same 16.37% rate as everyone else. The real tenure-side signal is manager continuity: leavers average 2.85 years with their current manager versus 4.37 for stayers.

The plan sequences spend against this concentration. In the first three months, the quick wins are governance, not money: overtime caps for JobLevel 1 and first-year staff, a ban on routine Sales Rep overtime, triage of the bottom-satisfaction scorers, and a rebuilt dashboard with OverTime as the top-level filter and rate-plus-count views so leadership stops steering by a misleading average. In months three to nine, targeted compensation does the heavy lifting: a pay floor for the <$2.5K band (fixing just 70 OT salaries saves ~36 exits), market benchmarks for the three bleeding roles, level-1 equity for the 631 zero-stock employees, a differentiated merit matrix for top performers, and structured first-year onboarding (~35 exits saved). Beyond nine months, structural fixes lock in the gains: a published L1-to-L2 progression framework, manager-continuity rules, reallocation of retention spend away from the already-safe 114 top earners, and tiered risk reporting as the permanent BI standard. These savings overlap and are not simply additive, but overtime normalization alone is worth ~84 exits (a 35% cut), and the combined program credibly moves company attrition from 16.12% toward the 11% range within 18 months — with nearly all spend focused on segments of 70 to 631 people rather than across-the-board programs.

kept.recommendation: Build a named 156-person retention list in the BI tool (OT flag AND JobLevel=1) with monthly manager review, OT caps, and accelerated level-2 promotion paths. Bringing this segment to the No-OT rate of 10.44% would save ~66 of its 82 leavers; even halving the rate saves ~41 exits per year.

kept.finding: Within overtime workers, PAY multiplies risk far more than attitude: OverTime + income under 2.5K churns at 68.57% (48 of 70) — the worst segment in the file — while OverTime + lowest job satisfaction (JobSat=1) churns at 'only' 35.71% (30 of 84). Low pay adds +38 points on top of the 30.53% OT baseline; low satisfaction adds just +5.2 points.
kept.numbers: OT+Income<2.5K: n=70, leavers=48, rate=68.57%; OT+JobSat=1: n=84, leavers=30, rate=35.71%; OT baseline=30.53%; Income<2.5K alone=34.07%; 2.5-5K band rate=16.44%
kept.so_what: Engagement surveys will systematically miss this problem — it is a compensation-structure issue, not a morale issue. Two out of three low-paid overtime workers walk out, effectively meaning the company pays to train their competitors' staff.
kept.recommendation: Prioritize a comp intervention for the 70 sub-2.5K overtime workers (overtime premium or raising base into the 2.5-5K band). At that band's 16.44% rate, expected leavers fall from 48 to ~12 — 36 saved exits from adjusting only 70 salaries, likely the highest ROI action in the entire analysis.

kept.finding: Sales Representative + OverTime is near-certain churn: 66.67% of this segment leaves (16 of 24), on top of a Sales Rep base rate that is already the worst of any role at 39.76% (33 of 83) — and Sales Rep leavers earn a median 2325 vs 2643 for stayers, a 12.0% pay gap.
kept.numbers: OT+SalesRep: n=24, leavers=16, rate=66.67%; SalesRep overall: n=83, leavers=33, rate=39.76%; median income leavers=2325 vs stayers=2643, gap=12.0%; role AvgMonthlyIncome=2626
kept.so_what: Two of every three overtime Sales Reps resign — the role combines lowest pay (avg 2626/month), high churn, and overtime load. This is a pipeline killer for the Sales department, which already runs the highest departmental attrition at 20.63%.
kept.recommendation: Ban routine overtime for Sales Representatives and fix the underlying territory/staffing ratio; pair with a pay-floor review given the 12% leaver pay gap. Even matching the role's own 39.76% base rate would save ~6 of the 16 segment leavers, and fixing the role overall protects an 83-person feeder pipeline for Sales Executive.

kept.finding: Business travel shows a clean dose-response curve: 8.0% attrition for non-travelers (12/150), 14.96% for rare travelers (156/1043), 24.91% for frequent travelers (69/277) — a 3.1x span — and layering Single marital status on frequent travel pushes it to 38.54% (37/96).
kept.numbers: Non-Travel: n=150, rate=8.0%; Travel_Rarely: n=1043, rate=14.96%; Travel_Frequently: n=277, leavers=69, rate=24.91%; chi2=24.2, p=5.61e-06; FreqTravel+Single: n=96, leavers=37, rate=38.54%
kept.so_what: Frequent travelers are 18.8% of the workforce but supply 29.1% of all leavers (69/237). The gradient proves travel burden itself — not who gets assigned travel — is the mechanism, so it is directly controllable through policy.
kept.recommendation: Cap consecutive travel assignments and rotate frequent-travel duty across the 1043-person rare-travel pool; go virtual-first for the 96 Single frequent travelers. Moving the 277 frequent travelers down to the rare-travel rate of 14.96% saves ~28 leavers per year.

kept.finding: Overtime in the first two years of tenure doubles new-hire loss: OverTime + Tenure<=2y churns at 50.96% (53 of 104), versus 34.88% for first-year employees overall (75 of 215) and 18.43% for the 2-3 year band — meaning the company loses every second new joiner it puts on overtime.
kept.numbers: OT+Tenure<=2y: n=104, leavers=53, rate=50.96%; first-year employees: n=215, leavers=75, rate=34.88%; tenure 2-3y band: rate=18.43%; mean YearsAtCompany leavers=5.13 vs stayers=7.37
kept.so_what: Onboarding investment is written off before payback: half of overtime-loaded new hires never reach year three. This silently inflates time-to-productivity metrics and recruiting spend.
kept.recommendation: Institute a no-overtime (or strict OT-cap) policy for the first 12 months of employment, with exceptions requiring HR sign-off. Bringing the 104-person segment to the general No-OT rate of 10.44% would save ~42 of its 53 leavers.

kept.finding: Work-life balance is a threshold effect, not a ladder: only the extreme-low group is dangerous — WLB=1 churns at 31.25% (25 of 80), 2.2x the WLB=3 rate of 14.22% — while the 'best' score WLB=4 actually churns HIGHER than WLB=3 (17.65% vs 14.22%), and the overall correlation is a weak -0.064, the lowest of all satisfaction metrics.
kept.numbers: WLB=1: n=80, leavers=25, rate=31.25%; WLB=2: 16.86%; WLB=3: n=893, rate=14.22%; WLB=4: n=153, leavers=27, rate=17.65%; pointbiserial WorkLifeBalance=-0.064; chi2=16.3, p=0.000973
kept.so_what: Broad company-wide wellbeing programs aimed at nudging everyone toward a '4' will not move attrition — the signal lives entirely in 80 people at the bottom. The non-monotonic top end suggests high-WLB scorers leave for other reasons entirely.
kept.recommendation: Replace blanket wellbeing spend with targeted triage: flag the 80 WLB=1 employees for immediate manager 1:1s and workload correction (they contain ~25 expected leavers). Cutting their rate to the WLB=3 level of 14.22% saves ~14 exits at minimal cost.

kept.finding: The full risk spread inside one company is 8.3x: the worst compound segment (OverTime + Income<2.5K, 68.57%) versus the safest (No OverTime + JobLevel>=3, 8.24%, 23 of 279) — the 16.12% headline average conceals populations with radically different realities.
kept.numbers: OT+Income<2.5K: rate=68.57% (48/70); No OT+JobLevel>=3: n=279, leavers=23, rate=8.24%; company average=16.12%; ratio 68.57/8.24=8.3x
kept.so_what: Reporting a single company-wide attrition KPI is actively misleading for decision-making: leadership sees a moderate 16% while specific 70-156 person pockets are hemorrhaging at 50-69%. Resource allocation follows the average and misses the fire.
kept.recommendation: Redesign the BI deliverable around risk tiers rather than one KPI: a tiered heat map (OT status x JobLevel x income band) with the No-OT senior segment (8.24%) as the internal benchmark, plus alerting when any segment exceeds 2x the company rate. This converts the dashboard from descriptive to operational.

kept.finding: First-year employees churn at 34.88% (75 of 215), meaning 14.6% of headcount (215/1470) generates 31.6% of all attrition (75 of 237 leavers) - the single steepest cliff in the tenure curve.
kept.numbers: TenureBand 0-1: n=215, leavers=75, rate=34.88%; company: n=1470, leavers=237, rate=16.12%; next band 2-3y rate=18.43%
kept.so_what: Recruiting and onboarding spend is being written off before it pays back: one in three new hires never reaches year two, and this cohort alone accounts for nearly a third of every exit the company processes.
kept.recommendation: Deploy a structured 30-60-90-day onboarding program with mandatory buddy assignment and quarterly stay-interviews in year one. Bringing the 0-1y rate down to the 2-3y band level (18.43%) would save ~35 exits per year and cut company attrition from 16.12% to roughly 13.7%.

kept.finding: Job Level 1 and Job Level 2 have almost identical headcounts (543 vs 534), yet L1 loses 143 people at 26.34% while L2 loses 52 at 9.74% - so L1 alone supplies 60.3% of all company attrition (143 of 237).
kept.numbers: JobLevel 1: n=543, leavers=143, rate=26.34%; JobLevel 2: n=534, leavers=52, rate=9.74%; 143/237=60.3% of total leavers
kept.so_what: Attrition is structurally concentrated at the entry level: the act of reaching Level 2 coincides with a 16.6-point drop in exit risk, so slow L1-to-L2 progression is effectively a churn generator for the majority of the workforce pipeline.
kept.recommendation: Publish a defined 18-24 month L1-to-L2 progression framework with skill milestones and mid-cycle promotion windows. Moving even a quarter of the L1 rate gap toward L2 behavior (~4 points off 26.34%) would retain ~22 additional employees per year.

kept.finding: Overtime turns early tenure into a near coin-flip: employees with OverTime and tenure of 2 years or less leave at 50.96% (53 of 104), versus 30.53% for all overtime workers and 10.44% for non-overtime staff; the OverTime + JobLevel 1 cell is worse still at 52.56% (82 of 156), which is 34.6% of all company attrition from one segment.
kept.numbers: OverTime+Tenure<=2y: n=104, leavers=53, rate=50.96%; OverTime overall: n=416, rate=30.53%; No OT: n=1054, rate=10.44%; OverTime+JobLevel1: n=156, leavers=82, rate=52.56%; 82/237=34.6%
kept.so_what: The company is burning out exactly the people it just paid to hire and train: half of new, junior, overtime-working staff walk out, compounding the first-year cliff and making one small segment responsible for over a third of total attrition.
kept.recommendation: Impose an overtime cap or manager sign-off rule for employees in their first two years and at Job Level 1, with a monthly BI alert listing junior staff exceeding overtime thresholds. Pulling the OT+L1 rate (52.56%) down to the overall L1 rate (26.34%) would save ~41 exits per year.

kept.finding: Promotion stagnation is a red herring for attrition: YearsSinceLastPromotion barely differs between leavers (mean 1.95) and stayers (mean 2.23, p=0.199, not significant, correlation -0.033), and the 116 veterans with 10+ years tenure and 7+ years without promotion churn at only 13.79% - below the 16.12% company average; the 107 promotion outliers (>7.5 years) churn at just 12.15%.
kept.numbers: YearsSinceLastPromotion: mean_leavers=1.95, mean_stayers=2.23, p=0.199, corr=-0.033; segment '10y+ tenure, 7y+ no promotion': n=116, leavers=16, rate=13.79%; outliers >7.5y: n=107, rate=12.15%; company rate=16.12%
kept.so_what: Retention budget aimed at promoting long-stagnant veterans to keep them is solving a problem the data says does not exist - those employees are already the most loyal cohort - while the actual flight risk (early-tenure, junior staff) goes underfunded.
kept.recommendation: Reallocate retention-promotion budget away from long-tenured stagnant employees toward first-two-year interventions, and instead manage the veteran group for engagement and knowledge transfer rather than flight risk. Expected impact: same spend, redirected at the 34.88% first-year cohort where each point of improvement saves ~2 employees.

kept.finding: Manager continuity, not promotion speed, is the relationship that predicts staying: leavers average 2.85 years with their current manager versus 4.37 for stayers (p=1.19e-10, correlation -0.156), and 2.9 vs 4.48 years in current role (p=3.19e-11, correlation -0.161) - both roughly 5x stronger correlates than YearsSinceLastPromotion (-0.033).
kept.numbers: YearsWithCurrManager: mean_leavers=2.85, mean_stayers=4.37, median 2 vs 3, p=1.19e-10, corr=-0.156; YearsInCurrentRole: 2.9 vs 4.48, p=3.19e-11, corr=-0.161; YearsSinceLastPromotion corr=-0.033
kept.so_what: Frequent manager reshuffles and team reorganizations reset the single strongest tenure-side loyalty bond in the data; an employee two years into a manager relationship is statistically in the leaver profile, while four-plus years matches the stayer profile.
kept.recommendation: Add 'manager changes in last 24 months' as a tracked risk flag in the attrition dashboard and require HR review before reassigning employees in their first two years under a manager. Realistic impact: protecting manager continuity for the 0-2y-with-manager population should shave 1-2 points off segment attrition given the 1.52-year mean gap.

kept.finding: Retention programs that target only juniors miss two-thirds of actual losses: leaver counts are almost identical across experience bands - Junior 75, Mid 82, Senior 80 - even though the rates collapse from 32.89% to 16.63% to 10.68%, because Senior headcount (749) is 3.3x Junior headcount (228).
kept.numbers: Junior (<5): n=228, leavers=75, rate=32.89%; Mid (5-9): n=493, leavers=82, rate=16.63%; Senior (10+): n=749, leavers=80, rate=10.68%; Mid+Senior = 162/237 = 68.4% of leavers
kept.so_what: Rate-based dashboards make attrition look like a junior-only problem, but in absolute replacement cost the company loses just as many mid-career (82) and senior (80) employees - who are far more expensive to replace - as juniors (75).
kept.recommendation: Build the BI dashboard to show absolute leaver counts alongside rates per experience band, and run three distinct playbooks: onboarding for Juniors, career-pathing for Mid (largest leaver group at 82), and knowledge-retention incentives for Seniors. Impact: addressing Mid attrition alone touches 34.6% of total losses.

kept.finding: Zero training is a cheap, high-signal risk flag: employees with 0 trainings last year churn at 27.78% (15 of 54) while a single training session coincides with a drop to 12.68% (9 of 71) - and leavers overall averaged fewer trainings than stayers (2.62 vs 2.83, p=0.0204).
kept.numbers: TrainingTimesLastYear 0: n=54, leavers=15, rate=27.78%; 1: n=71, leavers=9, rate=12.68%; 5: rate=11.76%; 6: rate=9.23%; means 2.62 vs 2.83, p=0.0204
kept.so_what: A group of only 54 people carries 1.7x the company attrition rate, and the biggest marginal gain in the entire training curve happens between zero and one session - signaling that total exclusion from development, not training volume, is what drives exits.
kept.recommendation: Institute a 'no employee at zero' rule: guarantee at least one training per year, with an automated HRIS report of anyone at zero trainings by Q3. If the zero-training cohort's rate fell to the one-training level (12.68%), that saves ~8 exits per year at the cost of ~54 training seats.

kept.finding: Attrition rebounds at the end of long careers: employees with 21+ years of tenure leave at 12.12% (8 of 66), nearly double the 6.67% (12 of 180) of the 11-20 year band, echoed by the 56-60 age band churning at 17.02% (8 of 47) versus 9.19% at 36-45.
kept.numbers: TenureBand 11-20: n=180, leavers=12, rate=6.67%; 21+: n=66, leavers=8, rate=12.12%; AgeBand 56-60: n=47, leavers=8, rate=17.02%; AgeBand 36-45: rate=9.19%
kept.so_what: These late-tenure exits are small in count but carry disproportionate institutional knowledge; the doubling of the rate after year 20 suggests unmanaged retirement-adjacent departures rather than the loyalty plateau the 11-20 band shows.
kept.recommendation: Launch a succession and knowledge-transfer program (documentation sprints, mentoring pairs, phased-retirement options) triggered at 20 years of tenure or age 55. With only 66 employees at 21+ tenure and 47 aged 56-60, full coverage is low-cost and converts unplanned exits into planned transitions.

kept.finding: Attrition collapses with age but is front-loaded to an extreme degree: employees aged 18-25 leave at 35.77% (44 of 123) versus 9.19% for ages 36-45 (43 of 468), and everyone 35 or under accounts for 160 of the 237 total leavers (44 + 116) — 67.5% of all attrition from 49.6% of headcount (123 + 606 = 729 of 1470).
kept.so_what: Two out of three replacement hires, onboarding cycles, and lost-productivity costs are generated by the under-36 population; the pipeline of future senior staff is draining before it matures, and each early exit forfeits the training already invested.
kept.recommendation: Build an early-career retention track (structured 12/24-month career-path conversations, mentor pairing, and accelerated first promotion review) for the 729 employees aged 35 and under. Closing even half the gap between the 18-25 rate (35.77%) and the 26-35 rate (19.14%) saves roughly 10 exits/year in that small band alone; a 3-point reduction across all 729 saves ~22 exits/year.

kept.finding: Single employees leave at 25.53% (120 of 470) — 2.5x the divorced rate of 10.09% (33 of 327) — and the file shows the 'No stock + Single' segment is exactly n=470 with 120 leavers at 25.53%, meaning every single employee holds StockOptionLevel 0, the level with the worst attrition (24.41%, 154 of 631).
kept.numbers: Single: n=470, 120 leavers, 25.53%; Divorced: 33/327, 10.09%; Married: 84/673, 12.48%; No stock + Single segment: n=470, 120 leavers, 25.53%; StockOptionLevel 0: 154/631, 24.41%; MaritalStatus chi2=46.2, p=9.46e-11
kept.so_what: Singles are 32% of the workforce but supply 50.6% of all leavers (120 of 237), and their risk is compounded — not coincidental — because none of them hold retention equity. The 'single employees just leave more' narrative masks a fixable equity-allocation gap. The overlap also worsens under load: OverTime + Single runs at 49.62% (65 of 131).
kept.recommendation: Audit stock/retention-award eligibility so grants follow role and performance rather than correlating with life stage, and extend Level 1-equivalent retention awards to high-performing singles. Level 1 holders leave at 9.4% (56 of 596); closing even one-third of the 16.1-point gap between singles at level 0 (25.53%) and level 1 (9.4%) would save ~25 exits/year.

kept.finding: Environment satisfaction shows a threshold effect, not a gradient: level 1 leaves at 25.35% (72 of 284), but levels 2, 3, and 4 cluster tightly at 14.98%, 13.69%, and 13.45% — so moving someone from 1 to 2 cuts risk by 10.4 points, while moving them from 2 to 4 gains only 1.5 points.
kept.so_what: Broad workplace-experience programs that nudge average scores upward are wasted spend; nearly all the attrition signal sits in the 284 people at rock bottom, who alone contribute 30% of total attrition (72 of 237 leavers).
kept.recommendation: Replace generic engagement initiatives with targeted remediation of the EnvSat=1 population: manager-led root-cause interviews and 90-day fix plans for that cohort only. Lifting them merely to level-2 conditions (14.98%) would cut their leavers from 72 to ~43 — about 29 saved exits/year, a 12% reduction in company-wide attrition.

kept.finding: Job involvement has the steepest satisfaction-family gradient in the file: level 1 leaves at 33.73% (28 of 83) versus 9.03% at level 4 (13 of 144) — a 3.7x spread, wider than job satisfaction (22.84% to 11.33%) and with a stronger point-biserial correlation (-0.13 vs -0.103).
kept.numbers: JobInvolvement 1: 28/83, 33.73%; level 2: 71/375, 18.93%; level 4: 13/144, 9.03%; JobSatisfaction 1: 66/289, 22.84%; level 4: 52/459, 11.33%; correlations: JobInvolvement -0.13, JobSatisfaction -0.103, WorkLifeBalance -0.064
kept.so_what: Disengagement from the work itself predicts exit better than dissatisfaction with the job's conditions — yet involvement is rarely tracked as a flight-risk KPI. The 83 low-involvement employees are a small, precisely identifiable group already producing 28 leavers.
kept.recommendation: Add JobInvolvement=1 as a red flag in the attrition dashboard and trigger a role-redesign or internal-mobility conversation within 30 days of scoring. Moving the level-1 group (33.73%) just to the level-2 rate (18.93%) saves ~12 exits/year from only 83 people — the highest per-capita return of any intervention in this dataset.

kept.finding: Work-life balance is non-monotonic: the worst score (level 1) leaves at 31.25% (25 of 80), but the best score (level 4) leaves at 17.65% (27 of 153) — higher than level 3's 14.22% (127 of 893).
kept.so_what: The assumption 'better balance always means better retention' fails at the top: employees reporting perfect balance leave 3.4 points more often than those reporting good balance, suggesting some are under-challenged or already detached. Meanwhile the 80 people at level 1 are the concentrated crisis, at nearly double the company rate of 16.12%.
kept.recommendation: Treat the two ends differently: workload rebalancing and overtime caps for the 80 WLB=1 employees (moving them to the level-3 rate of 14.22% saves ~14 exits/year), and stretch-assignment or growth check-ins for WLB=4 scorers rather than assuming they are safe.

kept.finding: Commute distance only bites beyond 10 km: attrition is flat at 13.77% (87 of 632) for 1-5 km and 14.47% (57 of 394) for 6-10 km, then jumps to 20.0% (48 of 240) at 11-20 km and 22.06% (45 of 204) at 21-29 km — the 444 employees beyond 10 km supply 93 leavers.
kept.so_what: The weak overall correlation (0.078) hides a real step-change: nearly 4 in 10 leavers (93 of 237) commute more than 10 km. A blanket commute policy would overpay the 70% who live close and under-serve the 30% actually at risk.
kept.recommendation: Offer hybrid/remote days or a transport allowance specifically to the 444 employees living 11+ km away. Bringing their blended rate (93/444 = ~21%) down to the 6-10 km rate of 14.47% would save ~29 exits/year; even a partial effect of one-third saves ~10.

kept.finding: Education field flags two hot pockets: Technical Degree holders leave at 24.24% (32 of 132) and HR-degree holders at 25.93% (7 of 27), versus 13.58% for Medical (63 of 464) and 14.69% for Life Sciences (89 of 606) — and the file's pay-gap table shows leaver underpayment in the roles these fields feed (Laboratory Technician leavers' median income 2,603 vs stayers' 3,068, a 15.2% gap; HR role leavers 2,652.5 vs 3,668.5, a 27.7% gap).
kept.numbers: Technical Degree: 32/132, 24.24%; HR field: 7/27, 25.93%; Medical: 63/464, 13.58%; Life Sciences: 89/606, 14.69%; EducationField chi2=16.0, p=0.00677; Lab Tech pay gap 15.2% (2603 vs 3068); HR role pay gap 27.7% (2652.5 vs 3668.5)
kept.so_what: Technically credentialed staff are the most market-mobile, and the pay-gap data shows their leavers were the underpaid ones — this is compensation-driven, poachable attrition, not disengagement. Technical Degree holders alone contribute 32 leavers, more than the entire HR department (12).
kept.recommendation: Run a market-pay benchmark for technical-degree-heavy roles (Lab Technician, Research Scientist) and correct below-median salaries first. Closing the gap enough to bring Technical Degree attrition (24.24%) to the Life Sciences rate (14.69%) would save ~13 exits/year from 132 people.

kept.finding: Gender is not a statistically meaningful attrition driver: males leave at 17.01% (150 of 882) versus females at 14.8% (87 of 588), but the chi-square test returns p=0.291 (chi2=1.1, flagged not significant in the file) — the only tested demographic dimension that fails significance.
kept.numbers: Male: 150/882, 17.01%; Female: 87/588, 14.8%; chi2=1.1, p=0.291, significant=false
kept.so_what: Dashboards that headline a male-vs-female attrition gap invite leadership to fund gender-targeted retention programs for an effect that is statistically noise, diverting budget from the drivers that are significant (marital/equity status p=9.46e-11, environment satisfaction p=5.12e-05, age).
kept.recommendation: Report gender as a monitoring dimension only, with the p-value shown, and reallocate any gender-specific retention budget toward the significant levers above; expected impact is cost avoidance and faster executive focus on the ~29-exit and ~25-exit opportunities rather than a 2.2-point gap that the data cannot distinguish from chance.

kept.finding: Laboratory Technicians are the single biggest absolute attrition drain: 62 of the company's 237 leavers (26.2%) come from one role of 259 people churning at 23.94%, and together with Research Scientists (47 leavers of 292, 16.1%) two R&D roles account for 109 of 237 leavers (46%).
kept.numbers: Lab Tech n=259, leavers=62, rate=23.94%; Research Scientist n=292, leavers=47, rate=16.1%; company leavers=237; Lab Tech AvgMonthlyIncome=$3,237.17; R&D dept rate=13.84%
kept.so_what: Dashboards ranked by rate alone point at Sales, but nearly half of all replacement/hiring cost sits in two low-paid R&D roles; ignoring them means retention spend misses the largest cost pool.
kept.recommendation: Launch a Lab Tech-specific retention program (pay progression + supervisor stability). Bringing Lab Tech attrition from 23.94% down to the R&D department average of 13.84% would save roughly 26 leavers per year, an 11% cut in total company attrition from one role.

kept.finding: Sales Representative is the most intense hotspot: 39.76% attrition (33 of 83), leavers earn a median of $2,325 vs $2,643 for stayers (12% gap), and the sub-segment working overtime loses 16 of 24 people (66.67%).
kept.numbers: Sales Rep n=83, leavers=33, rate=39.76%; median income leavers=$2,325 vs stayers=$2,643 (gap 12.0%); OverTime+Sales Rep n=24, leavers=16, rate=66.67%; AvgMonthlyIncome=$2,626
kept.so_what: The role effectively turns over its entire headcount every 2.5 years, destroying client relationships and pipeline continuity in Sales; two of every three overtime-working reps walk out.
kept.recommendation: Cap overtime for Sales Reps and raise the pay floor toward the stayer median (~$2,643). Cutting just the OT sub-segment to the overall Sales rate of 20.63% would save ~11 of those 16 leavers and pull the role below 30% attrition.

kept.finding: High performance provides zero retention protection: employees rated 4 leave at 16.37% (37 of 226), statistically identical to the 16.08% of rating-3 employees (200 of 1,244), and salary hikes are flat across outcomes (leavers 15.1% vs stayers 15.23% mean hike, p=0.614).
kept.numbers: Rating 4: n=226, leavers=37, rate=16.37%; Rating 3: n=1,244, leavers=200, rate=16.08%; PercentSalaryHike mean leavers=15.1 vs stayers=15.23, p=0.614; StockOptionLevel 0 rate=24.41% vs level 1 rate=9.4%
kept.so_what: The company is losing 37 documented top performers a year while its reward system (hikes) does not differentiate at all -- the costliest exits are being treated exactly like average ones.
kept.recommendation: Introduce differentiated retention for rating-4 staff, led by stock options: moving high performers from stock level 0 (24.41% attrition) to level 1 (9.4%) is associated with a ~15-point rate drop, which on 226 high performers could preserve 15-20 of the 37 annual losses.

kept.finding: Overtime is the strongest single lever and it compounds with low pay: overtime workers leave at 30.53% vs 10.44% without (chi2=87.6, p=8.16e-21), and the overtime + income<$2.5K segment loses 48 of 70 people (68.57%) -- the worst cell in the entire dataset.
kept.numbers: OverTime Yes: n=416, leavers=127, rate=30.53%; No: n=1,054, leavers=110, rate=10.44%; OT+Income<2.5K: n=70, leavers=48, rate=68.57%; OT+JobLevel1: n=156, leavers=82, rate=52.56%; 127 of 237 leavers (53.6%) worked OT while OT staff are only 28.3% of headcount
kept.so_what: Over half of all attrition flows through the 28% of staff working overtime; asking the lowest-paid employees for unpaid extra hours converts 2 of every 3 of them into leavers.
kept.recommendation: Enforce an overtime cap (or paid OT premium) for JobLevel 1 and sub-$2.5K earners first. Normalizing the OT+JobLevel-1 segment (82 leavers at 52.56%) to the no-OT rate of 10.44% would save on the order of 60+ leavers -- a quarter of total attrition.

kept.finding: The outliers section overturns the promotion-stagnation narrative: employees more than 7.5 years past their last promotion (n=107) leave at only 12.15%, below the 16.12% company average, and YearsSinceLastPromotion is statistically insignificant (leaver mean 1.95 vs stayer 2.23, p=0.199); meanwhile income outliers above $16,581 (n=114) almost never leave (4.39%).
kept.numbers: YearsSinceLastPromotion outliers: upper_fence=7.5, n=107, attrition=12.15%, p=0.199; MonthlyIncome outliers: upper_fence=$16,581, n=114, attrition=4.39%; segment '10y+ tenure, 7y+ no promotion': n=116, leavers=16, rate=13.79%; company rate=16.12%
kept.so_what: Retention budget aimed at long-stagnant senior staff is largely wasted -- they already stay; the real risk lives at the bottom of the pay scale, where leavers earn a mean of $4,787 vs $6,833 for stayers (p=4.43e-13).
kept.recommendation: Redirect any planned 'promotion fairness' retention spend toward the <$2.5K income band (34.07% attrition, 77 of 226 leavers), where each dollar addresses the segment with 8x the exit rate of top earners.

kept.finding: Sales has the worst departmental rate (20.63%, 92 of 446) but R&D supplies the most bodies: 133 of 237 total leavers (56.1%) come from R&D despite its below-average 13.84% rate, purely because it holds 961 of 1,470 employees.
kept.numbers: Sales: n=446, leavers=92, rate=20.63%; R&D: n=961, leavers=133, rate=13.84%; HR: n=63, leavers=12, rate=19.05%; total leavers=237, total n=1,470
kept.so_what: Rate-ranked reporting sends executives to Sales while 56% of replacement cost accrues in R&D; the BI dashboard must show rate and absolute count side by side or leadership will chronically misallocate.
kept.recommendation: Build the attrition dashboard with a dual-axis view (rate vs leaver count) and set department targets on absolute leavers: even a 2-point rate improvement in R&D (13.84% to 11.84%) saves ~19 people, more than a 4-point improvement in HR's 63-person department could.

kept.finding: Attrition is front-loaded and young: first-year employees leave at 34.88% (75 of 215), ages 18-25 at 35.77% (44 of 123), juniors with <5 years total experience at 32.89% (75 of 228), and adding overtime to tenure of 2 years or less pushes the rate to 50.96% (53 of 104).
kept.numbers: Tenure 0-1: n=215, leavers=75, rate=34.88%; Age 18-25: n=123, leavers=44, rate=35.77%; Junior (<5 yrs): n=228, leavers=75, rate=32.89%; OT+Tenure<=2y: n=104, leavers=53, rate=50.96%; tenure 11-20 rate=6.67%
kept.so_what: Roughly a third of every new-hire cohort is gone within a year -- recruiting spend leaks before onboarding investment pays back, and half of new hires asked to work overtime leave.
kept.recommendation: Institute a 12-month protection window for new hires: no overtime in year one plus structured 30/60/90-day check-ins. Cutting first-year attrition from 34.88% to the 2-3 year rate of 18.43% would retain ~35 additional employees annually.

corrections: [hotspots#2] The recommendation's 'saving 3-5 of the 12 annual exits' is not derivable from stats.json: lowering the HR role rate (23.08%, 12 of 52) to the cited department norm (19.05%) gives 52 x 0.1905 = 9.9 leavers, i.e. only ~2 exits saved, not 3-5. All other figures in the insight (HR dept 63/12/19.05%; HR role 52/12/23.08%; medians $2,652.50 vs $3,668.50; gap_pct 27.7; $1,016 gap; HR education field 25.93% = 7 of 27) are correct.
